articles.title: Hidden Gems Across America Found in Under-the-Radar Cities
articles.summary: A traveler who has visited all 50 US states prefers to explore lesser-known destinations for their unique charm.
articles.content: As I've traveled to all 50 states in the US, my experience has led me to seek out hidden gems rather than bustling metropolises. My preference for under-the-radar cities, towns, and villages stems from a desire to explore off the beaten path. These lesser-known destinations often possess a unique charm that is lost on more popular tourist spots. I've found myself drawn to places like Wickford Village in Rhode Island, which boasts a picturesque harbor setting and an abundance of independent shops and local eateries. For instance, Wickford Village is a beautifully maintained walkable community located just 30 minutes south of Providence in North Kingstown, Rhode Island. The village features a range of quality shops, including the nature-inspired World Store, and restaurants like Wickford on the Water. I've recently completed my quest to visit every US state, having traveled to my 50th destination earlier this year after decades of exploration. Since achieving this milestone, I've found myself turning down recommendations for major cities like Los Angeles or Miami in favor of more secluded spots. As someone who prefers to venture into the unknown, I'm naturally drawn to destinations that fly under the radar, such as a winter visit to Anchorage, Alaska, an experience that is both invigorating and unforgettable. Clinton, New York, has a distinctly charming atmosphere that feels like it's straight out of a postcard for small-town America. The village's main square boasts an array of independent shops and cafes, creating a picturesque scene reminiscent of a Hallmark holiday movie set. One of the standout features in Clinton is its coffee culture. The village is home to several excellent coffee shops, with Utica Coffee being one that stands out for serving some of the best maple lattes I've ever had. In addition to its coffee offerings, Clinton Cider Mill is another popular attraction, especially during the fall season when it's open from late August until Thanksgiving weekend. Visitors can indulge in fresh cider doughnuts that are simply delicious. The village's unique blend of natural beauty and quaint charm has left a lasting impression on me, making it an ideal destination to return to in the future, particularly for events like the Wickford Art Festival in July. As I sat on a bench, taking in the tranquil atmosphere of this charming village, I couldn't help but feel a sense of relaxation wash over me. The picturesque surroundings and quaint charm of the area had a profound effect on my mood, making it easy to unwind and soak up the serene ambiance. Walking through the village, I stumbled upon a series of stone cottages that looked like they belonged in a fairytale. These mushroom houses, built by local builder Earl Young, were not only visually stunning but also added to the whimsical charm of the place. Their unique design and architecture made them stand out as one of the most memorable aspects of my visit. I must admit that I had initially underestimated Fargo, North Dakota, assuming it would be a sleepy prairie town with little to offer. However, upon further exploration, I discovered a vibrant city with a walkable downtown area anchored by the iconic Fargo Theatre. This bustling hub was filled with life and energy, showcasing the city's hidden gems. One of my favorite experiences in Fargo was visiting Brewhalla, a brewery and food hall located in an industrial part of the city. The service was top-notch, and I appreciated the sense of community that permeated the atmosphere. It was clear that this spot had become a beloved gathering place for locals and visitors alike. As I reflect on my visits to various states, one destination that continues to hold a special place in my heart is Columbia, South Carolina. While it may not receive the same level of attention as some other popular spots in the state, I find myself drawn back to this charming city time and again. From its impressive zoo to its array of restaurants and parks, there's no shortage of attractions to explore in Columbia. As I wandered through the charming streets of Columbia, I was struck by its unique blend of Southern hospitality and vibrant culture. People from all walks of life seemed to be going about their day with a smile on their face, creating a warm and welcoming atmosphere that's hard to find elsewhere. In contrast to many other mountain cities in Colorado, Glenwood Springs stands out for its understated charm and natural beauty. As a native Coloradan, I've had the chance to explore many of the state's smaller towns, but there's something special about this one that keeps me coming back. The scenic drive into town via I-70 is an experience in itself, with breathtaking views of the Glenwood Canyon unfolding along the way. Although cell service can be spotty at times, it's a small price to pay for the stunning vistas on display. Once you arrive, downtown Glenwood Springs is easily navigable on foot, and its proximity to the Colorado River offers plenty of opportunities for outdoor exploration. In the winter, with a light dusting of snow still clinging to the trees, Glenwood Springs transforms into a serene and peaceful destination that's perfect for relaxation and rejuvenation. articles.title: Elsinore film revisits Ian Charleson's final months
articles.summary: The film Elsinore pays tribute to Scottish actor Ian Charleson's remarkable story through his struggles with a fatal illness while playing Hamlet at London's National Theatre.
articles.content: A new film, Elsinore, directed by Simon Stone, revisits the final months of Ian Charleson, a Scottish actor who rose to international stardom in Chariots of Fire but was struggling with a fatal illness when he took on the iconic role of Hamlet at London's National Theatre in 1989. The circumstances surrounding Charleson's performance were marked by secrecy and isolation, as young men in London were dying from AIDS in silence, often alone and without support. This tragic reality is now being remembered through Elsinore, a film that pays tribute to Charleson's remarkable story. It's impossible to know whether Hamlet was ever before played by an actor who understood the fragility of their own life. But what is clear is that Charleson's experience brought a unique depth and understanding to his portrayal of the character. Elsinore has been met with critical acclaim, with many praising Andrew Scott's performance as Ian Charleson in the film. Scott, an Irish actor known for his nuanced portrayals on screen, brings a level of authenticity to the role that has resonated with audiences worldwide. For Scott, acting is not about escaping reality but rather about exploring different aspects of himself. He believes that living can often feel like a kind of performance, and that the stage offers a promise of truth and authenticity. In an interview, Scott shared his insights on the nature of acting, suggesting that it's not about pretending to be someone else but rather about uncovering different facets of one's own personality. The film's exploration of Charleson's life and work serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of empathy and compassion in understanding the struggles of others. Elsinore is a poignant tribute to an actor who left an indelible mark on the world of theatre. The film Elsinore is a poignant tribute to an actor who left an indelible mark on the world of theatre. One scene that stands out is when Charleson, in his Hampstead flat, uses a blue plastic hand mirror to scan his body for signs of Kaposi's sarcoma, a condition associated with HIV and AIDS. This portrayal resonates deeply with Andrew Scott, who grew up in Dublin during the height of the AIDS crisis. He acknowledges that he was fortunate to have been born just a few years later than those who were most affected by the epidemic. As a result, he benefited from better education and treatment options. For men like Charleson's character, sex and death became inextricably linked due to the limited understanding of HIV at the time. articles.title: Mercury levels found in Pacific Coast marine mammals increase with predator status
articles.summary: Researchers led by Dr. Todd O'Hara have studied contaminant exposure in marine mammals and humans along the Pacific Coast, examining the impact on their health.
articles.content: Researchers studying marine mammals along the Pacific Coast of North America have found that contaminants such as mercury can move through marine food webs and become more concentrated as they move from prey to predator. This means that fish-eating marine mammals are exposed to higher levels of pollutants than other animals in their ecosystem. Dr. Todd O'Hara, a veterinary toxicologist at Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, has led research efforts along the Pacific Coast to better understand which contaminants marine mammals are being exposed to and what this exposure means for their health. His team's studies have included examining contaminant levels in marine mammals from Alaska to Mexico. The researchers' work also involves studying people who consume the same or similar fish as the marine mammals, allowing them to examine contaminant exposure across species that share marine food resources. This multi-species approach provides a more comprehensive understanding of the impact of pollutants on marine ecosystems. Seal and sea lion pups have become an important part of Dr. O'Hara's research because they can reveal insights into mercury exposure that begins before birth. Some contaminants can be transferred from mothers to their offspring during gestation and nursing, making young animals ideal subjects for studying early life exposures. A study led by Dr. O'Hara found that Steller sea lion pups from Alaska's western Aleutian Islands had higher concentrations of mercury and certain persistent organic pollutants than adult females and Steller sea lions from other locations. These pollutants include polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and the pesticide DDT, which have been banned in the United States for decades but can persist in the environment. The presence of these pollutants in sea lion pups suggests that they are being exposed to them through their mothers' milk or during gestation. This exposure can have long-lasting effects on the animals' health and may be linked to various health problems. The researchers' findings also highlight the importance of studying marine mammals from different locations to understand how contaminant levels vary across ecosystems. By examining contaminant levels in sea lion pups, Dr. O'Hara's team is gaining valuable insights into the impact of pollutants on marine life. Further research is needed to determine the full extent of mercury and other pollutant exposure among marine mammals along the Pacific Coast. The study's findings emphasize the need for continued monitoring and regulation of contaminants in the environment to protect both human and animal health. Research has shown that mercury levels in Steller sea lion pups vary depending on their location, likely due to differences in their mothers' diets. This highlights the crucial role maternal diet plays in determining exposure to contaminants before birth. Experts explain that regional variations in ocean currents and environmental conditions can shape local food webs and prey composition, which in turn affects maternal exposure to pollutants. As a result, pups from different areas may be exposed to varying levels of mercury and other elements through their mothers' milk. However, detecting the presence of mercury and other contaminants is only part of the story. Scientists also need to understand whether this exposure has any impact on the animal's functioning. This involves considering not just mercury, but also other elements like selenium that can interact with it and influence its effects on the nervous system and other organs. Researchers have noted that marine mammals, including pinnipeds such as seals and sea lions, are exposed to neurotoxic chemicals in much the same way as humans - through their diet. This means that understanding the effects of these chemicals is essential for protecting both human and animal health. A key challenge in studying the effects of neurotoxic chemicals on marine mammals is recognizing subtle neurological abnormalities. These can be difficult to identify, but may have serious consequences for animals in the wild. The anatomy of pinnipeds also makes it challenging to design a neurological examination that translates from other species. Their bodies are adapted for swimming and diving, with unique features such as flippers, reduced external ears, and thick layers of blubber. The researchers had to develop innovative methods to assess the neurological function of harbor seal pups, given their wild nature and aquatic environment. To create a standardized examination, the team collaborated with The Marine Mammal Center in California, where they worked on a tailored assessment specifically designed for harbor seal pups. Led by Dr. Christine Thomson, a veterinary neurologist, the research involved evaluating 45 stranded harbor seal pups over two years at the center. This comprehensive exam comprises 26 assessments that take into account the unique anatomy and behavior of pinnipeds. The examination enables veterinarians to thoroughly evaluate an animal's nervous system and pinpoint where abnormalities may be occurring, providing crucial information for diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. It also allows clinicians to distinguish between neurological disease and other non-toxic issues that might produce similar symptoms, such as ear infections or malnutrition. Some pups initially displaying abnormal neurological signs were later found to have underlying conditions like an ear infection, a congenital brain defect, or malnutrition, highlighting the importance of identifying these problems. Researchers studying the impact of mercury on marine mammals have found a way to compare naturally occurring exposure levels with neurological function in harbor seal pups. This distinction is crucial because detecting contaminants does not necessarily mean they are causing harm. The team, led by Dr. O'Hara, has been investigating how mercury affects pinnipeds, including seals, sea lions, and walruses. To examine this connection, researchers used neurological and clinical assessments to compare the effects of mercury exposure in harbor seal pups. These assessments allowed them to identify any adverse health effects caused by the contaminant. Dr. Marianne Lian's research, a former doctoral student of Dr. O'Hara's, found that fetal exposure to mercury was associated with differences in how harbor seal pups responded to touch and moved, as well as their rehabilitation needs. The study highlighted the difficulty of measuring adverse health effects in wild animals, where access to detailed neurological examinations can be limited. However, the findings provided valuable insights into the potential risks posed by prenatal mercury exposure. Researchers have found that fetal exposure to mercury before birth can lead to neurodevelopmental abnormalities in harbor seal pups. The standardized examination used to assess harbor seal pups is also a valuable tool for researchers studying the effects of mercury exposure. This method helps identify subtle neurological impairments that might otherwise go unnoticed and provides a consistent way to compare findings across animals and studies. Subtle neurological impairment can have significant consequences for an animal's survival in the wild, where being able to swim, navigate, and forage for food are essential skills. An animal may appear healthy while still having underlying neurological abnormalities that could impact its ability to survive after release from rehabilitation, according to O'Hara. The implications of this research extend beyond marine mammals and have important connections to human health as well. Since both humans and marine mammals rely on the same ocean resources, studying contaminants in these food webs can provide valuable insights into environmental risks affecting both species. O'Hara and his team are expanding their research to include more marine mammals and communities that depend on them for food. This will involve studying California sea lions in Mexico as well as continuing community-based participatory research involving harbor seals in Alaska. The focus of this work is on mercury and other trace elements, with a broader perspective provided by the One Health approach. The Texas A&M researchers involved in this project include Dr. Jill Hiney from the Department of Veterinary Integrative Biosciences, who has contributed expertise to the study. Additionally, Dr. Carlos Rosado Berrios, a postdoctoral researcher at VIBS, and retired faculty member Dr. Robert Taylor have also been part of the research team. The findings of this research will provide valuable insights into environmental risks affecting both humans and marine mammals that rely on the same ocean resources, ultimately contributing to better conservation efforts and public health policies. articles.summary: A meeting of Senate Republicans will take place on Tuesday to discuss their party's future and leadership strategy following midterm election losses.
articles.content: Senate Republicans are set to convene for an intense discussion about their party's future in the wake of the midterm elections that saw them lose control of the majority. The meeting, described as a "robust conversation, will take place on Tuesday and will focus on determining whether South Dakota Senator John Thune should remain as leader. Despite the losses, Thune is expected to retain his position due to his popularity among fellow Republicans and his unopposed candidacy. However, some Republican senators who returned to Washington after the election are calling for a reevaluation of their leadership strategy. Wisconsin Senator Ron Johnson has circulated a letter requesting a delay in the leadership elections, suggesting that the party needs to undergo significant changes following its defeat. Johnson acknowledged that there is currently no alternative candidate to challenge Thune's position, stating that that's part of our problem, who would want the job? The Republican Party is grappling with the aftermath of recent election losses, which have left many lawmakers uncertain about their future. Two crucial Senate contests remain undecided, pending the outcome of elections in Alaska and Mississippi. These results could further erode the party's numbers. Senate Republicans are set to proceed with internal elections, including leadership positions that will soon be up for grabs. However, some senators may still push for a delay in these proceedings as they convene on Tuesday morning. A consensus among party members is expected to emerge from this discussion. Thune has emphasized the need for a thorough examination of the party's current situation and its future trajectory. He plans to facilitate an open conversation with fellow senators about their next steps, which will ultimately be decided by the Republican conference as a whole. Thune has navigated complex relationships within his own party during his tenure as leader. The challenges facing Thune are not new, particularly in regards to his relationship with President Donald Trump. While Thune generally aligns with Trump's policy positions, he has resisted altering Senate rules or abolishing the filibuster to pass legislation requiring proof of citizenship for all voters. This stance has been met with frustration from some within Trump's base and the president himself. Despite his own reservations about Thune's potential leadership bid, President Trump has publicly expressed support for the senator, calling him a very fine man during a White House meeting last October. Thune's approach to leadership has been distinct from that of his predecessor, Mitch McConnell, with a focus on listening to diverse viewpoints and maintaining close relationships with rank-and-file senators. This emphasis on collaboration has earned Thune widespread respect within the party. Oklahoma Senator Jim Lankford has endorsed Thune for another term as Senate Republican leader, citing his broad support among GOP senators. Lankford noted that many of the newly elected senators will be in town for freshman orientation when the election takes place, making it a convenient time for the vote to occur. However, some Republicans are urging caution, arguing that the party should not rush into choosing a new leader without fully digesting the lessons of the recent elections. Pennsylvania Senator Dave McCormick has suggested that Republicans wait until after the two outstanding Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi have been decided before selecting their next leader. The outcome of the two remaining Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi remains uncertain, preventing a clear picture of the party's future leadership dynamics. As lawmakers strive to conclude this year's legislative business, they are focusing on essential tasks such as passing a government funding bill and finding common ground on specific issues like an energy permitting bill, which gained bipartisan support on Monday evening. The Senate is also working to confirm as many of President Trump's nominees as possible before the new Congress convenes on January 3. Meanwhile, Democrats will be strategizing about how to maintain their momentum into next year. In his initial remarks since the election, Senator John Thune emphasized that Republicans are willing to collaborate with Democrats but insisted that the American public is not seeking a socialist government or leftist fantasies." In the wake of election losses for the Republican Party, Senator John Thune has announced his intention to seek another term as Senate Republican leader. Several members of Schumer's party have expressed interest in challenging him, including Senators Chris Van Hollen and Elissa Slotkin. However, it seems they may not muster sufficient support to mount a successful challenge. Schumer's widespread popularity among his colleagues is evident from Senator Kirsten Gillibrand's prediction that he will secure enough votes for re-election. articles.title: National Guard Troops Could Be Called Away in War, Leaving States Vulnerable
articles.summary: Senior Army National Guard leaders expressed concern that a large-scale conflict with a major military power could drain troops from domestic emergencies.
articles.content: A major war abroad poses a significant threat to US states' ability to respond to emergencies at home, according to senior Army National Guard leaders who expressed concern about the potential drain on troops. The worry is that in the event of a large-scale conflict with a major military power, governors may find themselves without sufficient National Guard personnel to deal with natural disasters, cyberattacks, and other crises. This could leave states vulnerable to devastating consequences. The Guard's 329,000 soldiers would be stretched thin. Several generals discussed this issue at the Association of the United States Army's annual meeting in Washington last month, highlighting the dilemma that faces state governors. They pointed out that the Guard has a unique role, both responding to emergencies under the authority of state governors and serving as a combat reserve for the military. In such an event, large numbers of Guard troops could be called to active duty overseas, leaving governors with fewer personnel to handle domestic crises or protect critical infrastructure. The National Guard's dual role in both domestic and international conflicts has created a delicate balance of responsibilities. With thousands of Guardsmen currently deployed along the US southern border and in Washington D.C. to support an anti-crime initiative, states are already facing a strain on their resources. Furthermore, this year has seen a significant deployment of National Guard troops for overseas combat operations, such as Operation Epic Fury against Iran, while also responding to domestic emergencies like ice storms, hurricanes, and flash floods. This trend suggests that the Guard's capabilities may be stretched even thinner in the event of a major war. Maj. Gen. Larry Muennich, Indiana's adjutant general, has raised concerns about the potential consequences of mobilizing National Guard forces for war. He questioned what domestic emergency response capabilities governors would have left if their Guard troops were called away to fight overseas. Some states are proactively addressing this issue by taking steps to mitigate the potential shortfall in their National Guard resources. Florida has taken steps to mitigate potential gaps in National Guard resources by reviving its State Guard program. This separate, state-controlled volunteer force allows up to 1,500 volunteers to respond to emergencies within the state. Other generals have suggested implementing a process to resolve competing demands for troops between state and federal authorities. They also recommend improving civilian emergency response capabilities and streamlining mobilizations for certain home-defense missions. The National Guard's effectiveness in responding to crises is being closely watched by adversaries, according to Maj. Gen. Brey Hopkins. This scrutiny underscores the importance of developing strategies to ensure a robust and efficient military response in times of need.
